Gavrilo Princip, being arrested after his assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, which led to WW1. Sarajevo. 1914.

Gavrilo Princip (25 July – 28 April 1918) was a Bosnian who assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria and his wife, Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Princip and his accomplices, Yugoslav nationalists, were arrested and implicated several members of the Serbian military, leading Austria-Hungary to issue an unacceptable ultimatum to Serbia This was used as pretext for Austria-Hungary's invasion of Serbia, which then led to World War I.

As the Archduke and his wife drove through Sarajevo in an open top car, seven conspirators lined the route. The first failed to act but the second threw a bomb which missed the car and the other conspirators lost their opportunity to attack because of the heavy crowds and the car's high speed. To avoid capture, the bomb thrower swallowed a cyanide capsule and jumped into the Miljacka river to make sure he died. However, the cyanide pill was expired and only made him sick, and the river was only 10 centimetres (4 in) deep. A few seconds later he was hauled out and detained by police.

Later in the day Princip spotted the Archduke's car as it drove past, having taken a wrong turn. After realizing the mistake, the driver put his foot on the brake, and began to reverse. In doing so the engine stalled and the gears locked, giving Princip his opportunity. Princip stepped forward, drew his pistol, an FN Model 1910, and at a distance of about 1.5 metres (4.9 ft) fired twice into the car, first hitting Franz Ferdinand in the neck, and his wife in the abdomen. Princip attempted suicide with cyanide, but it was also expired, then tried to shoot himself, but the pistol was wrestled from his hand.

Princip was 19 years old and too young to receive death penalty. Instead, he received the maximum sentence of twenty years in prison. He was held in harsh conditions, which were worsened by the war, and died of tuberculosis about three years later.
